To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) attachment security in infancy is associated with competence and positive emotionality in childhood and adolescence and with the absence of psychopathology in adolescence; and that (2) attachment security in childhood and adolescence is associated with competence, positive emotionality, and the absence of psychopathic behavior in adolescence.

(a) early attachment security is a protective factor against subsequent psychopathology, (b) the protective effects of early attachment security operate in the context of current environmental supports, and (c) the effects of early attachment on later development are probabilistic, not deterministic.
attachment disorganization is associated with later psychopathology, and that attachment disorganization in turn is associated with early experience of maltreatment and with later maltreatment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of early attachment experience as a risk or protective factor in later psychopathology.
the interplay of attachment history, context, and developmental process in the emergence of developmental psychopathology.
how attachment theory can be used to understand the development of psychopathology and how psychopathology can be understood as an extension of normal development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
early anxious attachment is a risk factor for later psychopathology, but only when it is associated with other risk factors.
attachment theory is a developmental theory of psychopathological processes.
early attachment relationships are a major factor in the developmental process underlying psychopathology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

attachment security, as assessed by the Ainsworth Strange Situation procedure, is associated with a number of positive outcomes in the domains of social competence, academic achievement, and psychological adjustment.
the attachment system is a major organizer of human experience and behavior, and it is an essential component of the individual's adaptation to the environment.
the implications of attachment theory for psychopathology have been largely untested and underdeveloped.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the study of attachment in developmental psychopathological processes is not a simple matter.
attachment is a powerful lens for examining the development of psychopathology.
the study of psychopathology is not the study of the study of normal development, but rather the study of the normal developmental process in the context of risk and adversity.
